segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Another place where we use this mood tense is when we are giving orders to each other.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Most of the time, with just one exception which we will look at, we're using this mood tense to give orders.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: For example, if you wanted to say informally "don't speak",

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: you wouldn't say you don't speak, but you will put it in this mood tense. So how would you say that: "don't speak"?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: No hables. Good. "Don't speak": no hables.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: How would you say "don't stay"? "Don't stay" - still speaking informally. So you need to say you don't stay, and then you just switch the ending. So let's build it up together. How do you say "you don't stay"?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: No te quedas. So this is "you don't stay", but if you want to make this "don't stay", then you will use this mood tense.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: No te quedes. And then it sounds like "don't stay": no te quedes. "Don't stay here".

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good. No te quedes aquí. The word for "there" is ahí, ahí, spelled a-h-i.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: And there also exists allí spelled with double L. There's a tiny, even imperceptible difference between ahí (a-h-i) and allí (a-l-l-i).

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: How would you say "don't stay there" informally?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good. No te quedes ahí. Good.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: How would you say "don't give it"? Speaking informally: "don't give it".

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: No lo des. "Don't give it to him".

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Now, if you put a él, it's going to be for clarification purposes, in which case it will be a repetition of something else.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: No se lo des. Good. No se lo des. "Don't give it to him." What if you wanted to show, clarify, or emphasize that it's to him?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: No se lo des a él.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good. No se lo des a él. What was "to eat"?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Comer. Now, speaking to more than one person, how would you say "eat"? How would you tell more than one person to eat?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Coman. Good. So, how would you say "wait" talking to more than one person?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Now, if you want to say "wait for me" - we know already we don't use "for", we just say "me" (me) - with positive commands, with positive commands, when you're telling somebody to do something rather than not to do something, we have these little words like me or lo breaking the rules that we learned so far about their position. They will come after the changed verb, only with positive commands. This helps our ear tune in to the fact that it's a command, because other than that vowel changing, which is a very small change which might be quite hard to pick up audibly, we also have these small little words like me or lo coming after the verb, and that also helps our ear tune in to the fact that it's a command.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: So if you want to say to this more than one person, to this plural you, "wait for me", "await me", how will it sound?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Espérenme. Good. And it's written like one word as well: espérenme.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: How would you say "wait for it" or "wait for him", still to more than one person?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Espérenlos. But if you were to say "don't wait for them", then we don't have it on the end, this is a negative command. So "don't wait for them", still to more than one person?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Very good. No los esperen. How would you say, speaking formally, "eat"?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Cómalo. Good. So we have the lo on the end. But if you were to say "don't eat it", still speaking formally?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good. No lo coma. And speaking informally?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: No lo comas. And speaking to more than one person?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: No lo coman. But if we wanted to say "eat it", speaking to more than one person, positive command: "eat it"?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Olvidar, related to "oblivion" in English, actually. Oblivion means, uh, like a state of complete forgetting, so we can see the connection there between oblivion and olvidar. Olvidar, "to forget". Or olvidarse.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Either. It can be either because olvidar is a verb where we need to say what is being forgotten. We need to say it. So if we use "it", we have no problem: lo olvido. But if we want to just say "I forget", then we have a problem because we're not saying what, so we need to say "I forget myself": me olvido. So it's a verb that doesn't like to be alone.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: So how would you say "forget it", speaking formally: "forget it"?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Now, if we just want to say "forget", and we don't want to say "it", this verb doesn't like to be alone, so there we would say "forget yourself". So how would this be, still formally?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Very good. Olvídese. How would you say "don't forget it", speaking informally: "don't forget it"?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good. No lo olvides. But if we don't want to put the lo, we can just say "don't forget yourself", "don't forget". So how would that be?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good. No te olvides. Or we could do both. We could say no te lo olvides. We could put both: no te lo olvides.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: How would you say to more than one person, "don't forget", "you guys, don't forget"?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good. No se olviden. "Don't forget it", still to plural?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: No lo olviden. Good. Or no se lo olviden, you could put the both. Meaning doesn't really change.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: How would you say "let's not forget it"? How do you think that would be: "let's not forget it"?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good. No lo olvidemos. No lo olvidemos. But if you didn't want to say "it", and you just wanted to say "let's not forget", how would you say it?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: No nos olvidemos. Good. What was "to buy"?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Comprar. How would you say, to more than one person: "buy what is missing, what lacks, what is necessary"? So what was this missing, lacks, necessary verb?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good, faltar. So, speaking to more than one person, "buy what is missing, what is necessary, what lacks"?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good. Compren lo que falta. You could also say: compren lo que hace falta. "Buy what is making lack", you will hear that as well.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: So we're using the mood tense to make commands with one exception. The one exception is with positive informal commands. So what that means is when we're speaking informally and we're telling somebody to do something rather than not to do something. The reason why we don't use the mood tense here is because we want a shortcut. It's what we do most to tell people informally what to do.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: If you think about it, all day you're saying: "wait here", "buy this", "call me later", do that and the other, it's such common speech that it seemed a bit heavy to use the mood tense for this. So Spanish took a shortcut, and the shortcut is just dropping the S of the "you" form of the verb. So for example, we have comprar ("to buy"). "You buy" informally is?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Compras. Now to make the order, the positive order, we just drop the S and we get?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Which is the same as the he/she/it.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: It's the same as the he/she/it form, but it will never cause really any ambiguity for two reasons: firstly your tone of voice when you're making an order, the context is always very present, and also because we will be putting our small words like lo, me, la after the verb with the positive orders at least, so it's very obviously an order. But we want to think it through this way: that we are taking off the S so we keep the association with "you" informal. So, we have "to buy": comprar. "You buy" informally: compras. Then we want to make an order, we just get rid of the S and we say: compra.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: How would you say "buy it" talking informally?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Olvidar. How would you say "forget it" talking informally?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good, but we need to say what we're forgetting with this one.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Olvídalo. And if we don't want to say the lo, we can say?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Cómelo. Good. But "don't eat it", still informally?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: So it's just the positive commands that we have this shortcut. When we go to negative, we want to use the mood tense.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: No lo comas. Good. How would you say "eat it", speaking formally? Formally.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Cómalo. Good. "Don't eat it", still formally?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: No lo coma. Good. "Eat it", speaking plurally to more than one person: "eat it"?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: No lo coman. Very good. What was "to sell"?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: No lo vendas. So our shortcut is dropping the S of the present for the positive commands which are informal, huh? It's something that's quite specific: positive commands informally. But it's something that we do all day and that should help us remember that we have this shortcut for it.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Callar (c-a-l-l-a-r), callar means "to quiet", and callarse, callarse means "to shut up".

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: So how would you tell somebody to shut up informally?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: So is it as polite as "be quiet" or as rude as "shut up"?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: If you were to speak to more than one person, how would you say it?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Cállense. Good. Now we need the mood tense: cállense. Very good.
